config.title: Accessibility (a11y) Fundamentals

intro.title: Accessibility (a11y) Fundamentals
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a simple React form with TypeScript that demonstrates essential accessibility (a11y) practices. You'll learn core concepts like semantic HTML, ARIA attributes, and keyboard navigation to make web applications usable for everyone. The main technologies involved are React components, TypeScript for type safety, and HTML accessibility features. By the end, you'll understand how to create inclusive interfaces that work with screen readers and other assistive technologies.
intro.usecase: Accessibility (a11y) fundamentals are essential for building inclusive software used by millions, such as e-commerce checkout forms, banking dashboards, and social media feeds. In real products, developers implement semantic HTML, ARIA attributes, and keyboard navigation to ensure features like search filters, data tables, and modal dialogs are usable for people with disabilities. For example, a React dashboard with interactive charts must provide screen reader support and focus management so all users can analyze data. Mastering these patterns helps you create applications that comply with legal standards like WCAG and reach a broader audience in professional scenarios.

objectives: Implement semantic HTML elements in React components to improve screen reader navigation
Apply ARIA attributes to enhance accessibility for dynamic content
Configure keyboard navigation handlers for interactive components
Construct accessible form controls with proper labeling and validation feedback
Update component focus management to maintain logical tab order
Integrate screen reader announcements for state changes and notifications
Manipulate component visibility to support assistive technologies

steps.title: Import React and useState
steps.instruction: Import React and the useState hook from 'react'.
steps.hint: Use the import statement to bring in React and useState from the 'react' package.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: importing React and a hook
import React, { useState } from 'react';
steps.expectedOutcome: The imports are added at the top of the file, enabling you to use React and state management.
successCriteria: React and useState are imported from 'react'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're importing both React and useState from 'react'. Check your import statement syntax.
steps.feedbackWrong: import React and useState from the 'react' package using the import statement.

steps.title: Create main App component
steps.instruction: Create a functional component named App that returns JSX. Use TypeScript to type the component.
steps.hint: Define a function or arrow function named App that returns some JSX, like a div with a heading.
steps.seedCode:
import React, { useState } from 'react';

// Create the App component here
steps.expectedOutcome: The App component is defined and returns JSX.
successCriteria: A functional component named App exists and returns JSX.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've created the main App component.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you define a component named App that returns JSX.
steps.feedbackWrong: The App component is not defined correctly. Check the component name and return statement.

steps.title: Initialize state for toggle visibility
steps.instruction: Inside the App component, initialize a state variable named 'isVisible' using useState. Set its default value to true and include the proper TypeScript type annotation.
steps.hint: Use the useState hook you imported earlier. Remember to specify the type as boolean for TypeScript.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: boolean state with TypeScript
const [isActive, setIsActive] = useState<boolean>(true);
steps.expectedOutcome: The App component will have a boolean state variable 'isVisible' initialized to true with proper TypeScript typing.
successCriteria: State variable 'isVisible' is declared using useState
Default value is set to true
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you've included the TypeScript type annotation <boolean> and set the default value to true.
steps.feedbackWrong: use useState with the boolean type and initialize isVisible to true inside the App component.

steps.title: Define toggle handler function
steps.instruction: Inside your App component, define a function named toggleVisibility that toggles the isVisible state value.
steps.hint: Use the setter function from useState to update the state. You can toggle a boolean by returning the opposite of its current value.
steps.expectedOutcome: You should have a toggleVisibility function that uses setIsVisible to toggle the isVisible boolean state.
successCriteria: A function named toggleVisibility is defined inside the App component
The function toggles the isVisible state using setIsVisible
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've defined a function, but make sure it toggles the isVisible state correctly.
steps.feedbackWrong: The toggleVisibility function isn't defined correctly. Check the function name and toggle logic.

steps.title: Add main container with semantic heading
steps.instruction: Inside your App component's return statement, replace the current return value with a <main> element that contains an <h1> heading with the text 'Accessibility Fundamentals'.
steps.hint: Use JSX to create a <main> element and nest an <h1> inside it. The <main> element is a semantic HTML5 tag that helps screen readers identify the primary content.
steps.expectedOutcome: The App component returns a <main> element containing an <h1> with the specified text, establishing a semantic structure for the page.
successCriteria: The component returns a <main> element that contains an <h1> with the exact text 'Accessibility Fundamentals'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure the <h1> is nested inside the <main> element and has the exact text 'Accessibility Fundamentals'.
steps.feedbackWrong: The structure doesn't match the requirement. Please ensure you return a <main> element containing an <h1> with the text 'Accessibility Fundamentals'.

steps.title: Add accessible button with ARIA attributes
steps.instruction: In your component's return statement, add a button element with the following: an onClick handler that calls toggleVisibility, an aria-label attribute set to 'Toggle content visibility', and type='button'.
steps.hint: Remember to define the toggleVisibility function first if you haven't already. The aria-label provides an accessible name for screen readers.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: accessible button with ARIA attributes
<button 
  onClick={handleClick}
  aria-label="Submit form"
  type="button"
>
  Submit
</button>
steps.expectedOutcome: The button will be added to the UI with proper accessibility attributes and event handling.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure your button has all required attributes: onClick, aria-label, and type='button'.
steps.feedbackWrong: The button doesn't meet all accessibility requirements. Check that it has onClick, aria-label, and type='button' attributes.

steps.title: Add conditional content with ARIA live region
steps.instruction: Inside your component's return statement, add a <div> element with the aria-live='polite' attribute that conditionally renders content based on the isVisible state.
steps.hint: Use a ternary operator inside the div to show different text when isVisible is true or false. Remember to include the aria-live attribute for screen reader announcements.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will include a div with aria-live='polite' that announces dynamic content changes to screen readers when the visibility state changes.
successCriteria: A div element with aria-live='polite' attribute is added that conditionally renders content based on isVisible state using a ternary operator.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added the conditional content, but make sure to include the aria-live='polite' attribute on the div element for proper screen reader announcements.
steps.feedbackWrong: The conditional content with ARIA live region wasn't added correctly. Review how to add aria-live attributes and conditional rendering in React.

steps.title: Add form with accessible labels
steps.instruction: Inside the main container, add a form element with an input field and a label. Use the htmlFor attribute on the label and matching id on the input to associate them.
steps.hint: The label should have htmlFor set to a unique id, and the input should have the same id value. This ensures screen readers can properly announce the input's purpose.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of accessible form label association
<form>
  <label htmlFor="nameInput">Name:</label>
  <input id="nameInput" type="text" />
</form>
steps.expectedOutcome: A form with properly associated label and input elements will be added to the main container, demonstrating accessible form labeling.
successCriteria: A form element is added containing a label with htmlFor and an input with matching id.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you have both a label with htmlFor and an input with matching id inside a form element.
steps.feedbackWrong: The form or label association is missing. Review the example and ensure you're using htmlFor on the label and matching id on the input.

steps.title: Add focus management example
steps.instruction: Inside the main container, add a button with autoFocus and tabIndex attributes for focus management.
steps.hint: Add a <button> element with autoFocus={true} and tabIndex={0} attributes. Include descriptive text like 'Focus example button'.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: button with focus attributes
<button autoFocus={true} tabIndex={0}>
  Focus example
</button>
steps.expectedOutcome: A button with autoFocus and tabIndex attributes appears in the main container.
successCriteria: The button includes autoFocus={true} and tabIndex={0} attributes with descriptive text.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You added a button, but it's missing either autoFocus or tabIndex attributes. Both are needed for proper focus control.
steps.feedbackWrong: The focus management button wasn't added correctly. Check that you've included both autoFocus and tabIndex attributes on a button element.
